rv.q: Indhu Rubasingham's wonderful production of The Father and the Assassin puts on stage an important piece of history, an arresting personal story and a vital, distinctive theatrical language.

It's a tremendous piece of writing from Chandrasekhar and a titanic lead performance from Saraf: part historical character study, part meta-comedy, part philosophical treatise, part forensic analysis of colonialism's legacy and nationalism's toxicity.
The Father and the Assassin successfully weaves a thorny mass of contentious history and factional politics into a tight and accessible drama.

Anupama Chandrasekhar artfully unpicks the forces of history with a tale of violence and colonialism that echoes into today. It needs a powerful actor to hold the centre as Godse, and in Shubham Saraf it gets one.
Our populism-blighted present hovers over Chandrasekhar’s play as it presents us with the story of Godse, and of the painful birth of modern India.
No question, this is a fascinating, important evening, with valuably shaming moments of British imperial brutality referenced en route and a topical sting in the tale about rising intolerance.
Indhu Rubasingham's two-and-a-half hour jaunt through half a century of Indian political history is always entertaining.
The play is heavy on exposition but oddly short on dramatic substance.
Shubham Saraf imparts just about enough craziness into Godse to save the show from becoming an apologia for Islamophobia.
Despite its playful flourishes and some eye-catching set pieces, it's a stolid evening.
Abeysekera’s command of the Olivier stage is effortless, bringing real intimacy to a sweeping production and a presence that is both tough and effeminate, a small man determined to make a big impact.
It is a star-making performance in an ideal production of a play that turns a foregone conclusion into a dynamic evening of inevitable history that plays as a succession of surprises.
It makes bold and invigorating theatre that is discreetly underlined by Siddhartha Khosla's music which rises to a dramatic crescendo when partition is presented.
This is a history play, the modern resonances abound without ever being spelt out.
It is his performance, under Indhu Rubasingham's sure direction, which sets the tone.
Never mind. It's worth a visit.
The Father and the Assassin is a mixed bag, elevated by Saraf's central performance.
Surprising in terms of its themes, there are some real laugh-out-loud lines of dialogue along with more powerful moments as the differing attitudes towards Partition are explored.
